Liraglutide significantly reduced the incidence of this primary MACE outcome by 13% compared with placebo (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.78–0.97) [5][6][9]. In pooled analyses of SUSTAIN 6 and PIONEER 6, semaglutide significantly reduced primary MACE (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62–0.92, p = 0.0062) and expanded MACE (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.68–0.95, p = 0.0097), with the effect independent of baseline cardiovascular risk except in people with prior heart failure [1][4][9].

answer: GLP-1 receptor agonists are proposed to reduce cardiovascular events primarily through indirect mechanisms, including weight loss, blood pressure reduction, improved glycemic control, and anti-inflammatory effects [1]. Additional indirect contributions include improvements in lipid metabolism (reductions in triglycerides and small, dense LDL particles), attenuation of atherogenic dyslipidemia, and amelioration of endothelial dysfunction [2], as well as reduced oxidative stress and inhibition of myocardial cell apoptosis [7]. Direct mechanisms have also been proposed, such as improved myocardial perfusion through endothelial modulation, antifibrotic effects on myocardial tissue, reduced epicardial adipose tissue, modulation of the autonomic nervous system toward parasympathetic activity, and promotion of natriuresis and diuresis [1]. Antithrombotic effects—comprising platelet inhibition, augmented fibrinolytic responses, and attenuated thrombogenesis—represent a further proposed direct cardiovascular protective mechanism [6]. Meta-regression data indicate that both systolic blood pressure and weight reductions are independently associated with MACE risk reduction, with the cardiovascular benefits likely influenced by both [5].

answer: Both drug classes reduce cardiovascular risk in type 2 diabetes, but their benefit profiles differ by outcome rather than showing uniform superiority: SGLT2 inhibitors primarily reduce heart failure hospitalisation, whereas GLP-1 RAs mainly reduce stroke and myocardial infarction [6]. Consistent with this, a real-world cohort found a significantly lower rate of heart failure admissions with SGLT2 inhibitors (6.0% vs 10.6%) and a slightly superior overall MACE profile, while GLP-1 RAs primarily reduce atherosclerotic events [7][10]. Prior meta-analyses have yielded conflicting results, with some reporting greater heart failure reduction with SGLT2 inhibitors and others more robust MACE reduction with GLP-1 RAs, so it remains unclear whether either class provides superior overall cardiovascular protection [5]. The two classes have distinct but potentially synergistic mechanisms, and combination therapy may produce additive improvements in HbA1c, blood pressure and body weight, though effects on cardiorenal outcomes remain uncertain [1][6].

answer: The safety profile of GLP-1 RAs regarding pancreatitis is mixed: large cardiovascular outcome trials and subsequent meta-analyses have not demonstrated a statistically significant increase in acute pancreatitis compared with placebo, and no significant increase in acute pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer has been reported [1][4][9]. However, a large retrospective cohort study found that GLP-1 RA use was associated with a small increased risk of acute pancreatitis (HR 1.058, 95% CI 1.015–1.103), with the excess risk more pronounced during the first 6 months of treatment, while no differences were observed for chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer [5][6][10]. Preclinical studies and pharmacovigilance reports have suggested a possible association with pancreatic diseases, though these risks remain unconfirmed as clinical trials were not powered to assess pancreatic safety [3]. Additionally, emerging case reports and pharmacovigilance data indicate that structural pancreatic abnormalities, including mucinous cystic lesions, may develop independently of pancreatitis [2]. GLP-1 RAs should therefore be used with caution in patients with a history of pancreatitis [9].

answer: Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist rather than a selective GLP-1 receptor agonist, engineered as a single 39-amino acid peptide that activates both receptors [4][8]. It exhibits balanced agonism at GLP-1R with a fivefold higher affinity for GIPR, and combined receptor activation produces supra-additive cAMP generation, larger first-phase insulin release, and enhanced adiponectin-mediated lipid oxidation [2]. Concurrent GIPR stimulation amplifies insulin release via PI3K–AKT signalling and, in preclinical models, supports β-cell proliferation and survival, with in vitro supra-additive β-cell cAMP and insulin secretion compared with GLP-1 or GIP alone [10]. This dual mechanism augments insulin secretion, improves insulin sensitivity, enhances lipid metabolism, and facilitates greater weight reduction than GLP-1 monotherapy [1][8]. Consequently, tirzepatide achieves larger reductions in body weight and visceral/ectopic fat, though these additional weight-loss effects do not necessarily translate into further cardiovascular outcome benefits versus selective GLP-1 receptor agonists [1][6].
